blocks.h: Why high bits first, low bits for the rest?
p: `x XOR num1` has a 1 wherever the two differ. A difference in a high bit costs far more than any number of low-bit differences. So the best `x` agrees with `num1` on its highest set bits (making those XOR to 0) and, if more bits are needed, places the extra bits in the lowest positions.

blocks.h: Why track the remainder rather than the full sum?

The 'minimum number of powers of 2 that sum to n' is exactly the set bits
Multiply the range, reducing modulo 10⁹ + 7 each time

p: Since every element is a power of two, the product of a range is `2` to the power of the sum of the exponents, computable with a prefix sum of bit positions and one `pow(2, e, MOD)`. This code multiplies directly, at most 30 numbers per query, which is fast enough.

2438.takeaway: Range products of powers: the powers are the set bits of n; multiply the queried slice modulo 10⁹+7.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: Seeding target `s` destroys every target `t` with `t ≡ s (mod space)`, `t ≥ s`; so targets with the same remainder form a class
`min(x for x in nums if cnt[x % space] == top)`
Seed the SMALLEST number in a best class, since the smallest one destroys all the others in the class
Smallest value on ties between classes

p: The class with remainder 1 has 5 numbers (3, 7, 1, 1, 5); its smallest member is 1, so seed 1.

blocks.h: Why the smallest member of the class?
p: Seeding `s` destroys `s, s + space, s + 2·space, …`, so seeding the smallest member of a class destroys every other member (they are all larger by a multiple of `space`). Any larger seed would miss the smaller members.

bullets: Space: O(space) in the worst case.

2453.takeaway: Destroy sequential targets: group numbers by remainder mod space; seed the smallest number of the largest group (smallest overall on ties).

blocks.h: Why is the cost per edge independent?
p: Every representative in a subtree must cross the edge above it, and cars can carry `seats` people. Merging people into full cars as early as possible is optimal, so the cars needed on an edge is exactly ⌈people / seats⌉, and edges don't interact.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: If the shop closes at hour 0, every customer who would come (`Y`) is a penalty
Moving the closing time past hour `i`: an `N` hour now counts as 1 (open with no customer), a `Y` hour removes 1 (customer served)
A strictly smaller penalty at hour `i + 1`
Strict `<` keeps the EARLIEST closing time on ties

p: `"YYNY"`: closing at hour `h` means open for the first `h` hours.

blocks.h: Why can the penalty be updated incrementally?
p: Penalty(h) = (number of `N` in the first h hours) + (number of `Y` in the remaining hours). Extending the open period by one hour moves that hour from the second group to the first: `+1` if it was `N`, `−1` if it was `Y`.

2483.takeaway: Best closing time: start with penalty = number of Y, then sweep, adding 1 for N and subtracting 1 for Y, keeping the earliest minimum.

rows: Prefix counts of zeros and ones
A substring has `zeros : ones = num1 : num2` iff `zeros·num2 = ones·num1`; for a substring between two prefixes this means their keys are EQUAL
Turn a ratio condition into an equality of a linear key

blocks.h: Why do equal keys mean the right ratio?
p: For a substring `s[i..j]`, zeros = `z_j − z_i` and ones = `o_j − o_i`. The condition `zeros·num2 = ones·num1` rearranges to `(z_j·num2 − o_j·num1) = (z_i·num2 − o_i·num1)`, i.e. the keys of the two prefixes are equal. The same trick solves 'equal number of 0s and 1s' (num1 = num2).

2489.takeaway: Substrings with a fixed 0:1 ratio: prefix key z·num2 − o·num1; count pairs of equal keys with a hash map.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: After enough days every number `2..n` appears on the board; `1` appears only if `n = 1`
Each day, a number `x` on the board adds every `i` with `x % i == 1`

p: `n = 5`: start with `{5}`. Since `5 % 4 == 1`, 4 is added; then `4 % 3 == 1` adds 3; `3 % 2 == 1` adds 2. After enough days the board is `{2, 3, 4, 5}`, four numbers.

blocks.p: For `x ≥ 3`, `x % (x − 1) == 1`, so each day the smallest number `x` on the board adds `x − 1`. The chain ends at 2: the remainder rule never produces 1 (that would need `x % i == 1` with `i = 1`, but `x % 1 = 0`). The board therefore ends as `{2, …, n}` which has `n − 1` numbers when `n ≥ 2`, and is just `{1}` when `n = 1`.

2549.takeaway: Count distinct numbers on the board: the process adds n−1, n−2, …, 2, so the answer is max(1, n − 1).
